title: Secret Code Lab
goal: Your kid learns to make and crack real codes. They break an easy one, find out how a key works, invent their own, crack a message with no key at all, then keep a code going with someone for a week and see how the same idea protects real secrets.
need: Someone to swap coded messages with

academics.subject: Math
academics.text: counting, patterns and shifting by a number

academics.subject: History
academics.text: real codes and the people who broke them

academics.subject: Digital Literacy
academics.text: what keeps passwords and messages safe

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: You don't need to know anything about codes. You write the first one, you get stuck on theirs, and when they're stuck on yours, you wait. Getting stuck is the whole thrill. Your most useful question is 'What gave it away?' Put something worth reading in the message too, like a compliment or where the cookies are.

plan.what: Crack the first code and make a key (Steps 1 and 2).
Invent a code and break one with no key (Steps 3 and 4).
Swap coded notes, then talk about real secrets (Step 5).

troubleshoot.a: Give one letter away, and only one. Solving the rest themselves still counts, and one letter is often all it takes.
That's the good part. Go through it together, letter by letter, and find the slip. Codes are unforgiving, so they get careful quickly.

troubleshoot.q: They want to keep secrets from me
troubleshoot.a: Enjoy it, and say the rule out loud once: surprises and silly secrets are fine, and a secret that worries you or hurts someone is always one to tell.

lesson.text: Every code is a rule and a key. A good one is easy if you've got the key and hard if you haven't, and there's always something in it that can give it away.
lesson.before: I wrote it backwards. Nobody will ever get it.

model.line: Move every letter along the alphabet.
The number 3, so A becomes D.

lesson.modelNote: Backwards takes one good look. This one needs the key or a lot of patience, though the double H is where a codebreaker would start.

steps.title: Crack your first code
steps.why: One quick win and they'll want a harder one.
steps.kid: You hand your kid a short coded message, and they work out the trick. They look for what's strange about it, try an idea and read the message. Then they say out loud exactly what the rule was.
steps.you: Write a short message using something from the Starter codes card in the Code Toolkit at the end of the guide. Make it easy enough to crack in a minute or two, and make it worth reading.
steps.tip: Slide it under a door or hide it in a shoe. It's much more exciting than handing it over.

levels.explore: Crack three words using a chart where a picture stands for each letter.
levels.develop: Crack a backwards or number code, with no help.
levels.extend: Crack a one-along code and explain the exact rule.

steps.title: Make a key
steps.why: A code is a rule. The key is what opens it.
steps.kid: Your kid writes out the alphabet with a code alphabet underneath, shifted along by a number. They lock a message with it and unlock one from you. Then they try a different number and see what happens to the same message.
steps.you: Show them the chart once, then tell them about Caesar: his letters used a shift of 3, so A became D. Ask what happens at the end of the alphabet, and let them work it out.
ask: Who can read this if they don't have the number?
steps.tip: Cut two strips of paper with the alphabet on each and slide one along. Now they can see the shift.

levels.explore: Use a shift of 1 to write your name, with the chart in front of you.
levels.develop: Make a chart for any number, then code and decode a sentence.
levels.extend: Swap messages using a new number each time, and explain why the number has to stay secret.

steps.title: Invent your own
steps.why: Writing a code is harder than reading one, because one slip breaks it.
steps.kid: Your kid chooses or invents a code, using the Stronger codes card, and fills in My code at the end of the guide. They write you a real message and hand it over with the key. If it doesn't decode, they find the slip.
steps.you: Be the one who has to read it, slowly and honestly. Say where you got stuck. Ask if it would still be easy to use when they're in a hurry.
ask: Is it easy with the key and hard without it?
Where would someone start if they wanted to break it?
steps.tip: Have them code the message twice. If the two don't match, they've found their slip.

levels.explore: Make a symbol for ten letters, and write a short word for someone to read.
levels.develop: Invent a key for the whole alphabet and code a full sentence with no mistakes.
levels.extend: Build a keyword code or pigpen, then write a message long enough to be worth breaking.

steps.title: Break one with no key
steps.kid: You give your kid a coded message and no key. They use the Crack-in clues card: they count which symbol shows up most, look at the short words and the doubles, and pencil in a guess. They keep testing until the whole thing opens up.
steps.you: Write three or four long sentences, because short ones don't have enough clues. Then tell them that over a thousand years ago, a scholar in Baghdad named al-Kindi wrote down this very method.
ask: Which one shows up the most?
If that's an E, what else has to be true?
steps.tip: Guess in pencil. Being wrong about one letter is how they find out what the right one is.

levels.explore: Crack a short code with half the letters already filled in.
levels.develop: Count the letters and break a shift code with no key.
levels.extend: Break a code where any letter can stand for any other, using counts and short words.

steps.title: Keep a secret for real
steps.why: The same idea is guarding real things right now.
steps.kid: Your kid picks someone and swaps coded notes for a week, keeping the key private. Then they look at the Real secrets card with you, and work out what the key is in each one. They explain to someone how a password is like a key.
steps.you: Show them the lock beside a web address and explain that what you send gets scrambled on the way. Talk about your own rules for passwords. Real codes are far harder than these, and the big idea's the same.
ask: What would happen if somebody got yours?
steps.tip: Leave notes in odd places all week. The fridge, a boot and a cereal box all work.

levels.explore: Leave three coded notes this week, and say why a password stays private.
levels.develop: Swap notes for a week, then explain how your code and a password are alike.
levels.extend: Change your key halfway through without giving it away, then explain why real systems change keys too.

skills.text: finding the rule in a jumble

skills.name: Persistence
skills.text: staying with it until it opens

conclusion.headline: They looked at a jumble and found the rule.
conclusion.text: Watch for it in the weeks after. If they ask how a password works, spot a pattern on a sign or leave you a message you can't read, it's stuck.
conclusion.celebrate: The next time they crack something hard, say: 'You didn't have the key, and you got in anyway.'

signs: They look for the rule when something's confusing

They keep their passwords to themselves
makeItReal: Choose a family code and use it for birthday notes, surprises and where the cookies are hidden.

fromHome.text: Every Easter, I make a treasure hunt for my kids with codes in the clues. Then they make one for us parents, and we're the ones stuck at the table.
